entries.source_use: California recommendation that schools set reunification locations and procedures and tell parents in languages they understand.

source_records.supports: California's state education agency recommends that schools establish reunification locations and procedures and ensure parents and guardians are aware of them, and that schools inform parents in languages they understand of reunification plans and the necessity of cooperating with first responders; it also lists required safety-plan components, which this guide does not reproduce.

entries.source_use: Do not go to your children unless officials say it is safe; they may be sheltered where they are.

source_records.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
source_records.supports: In some chemical emergencies staying put and sealing off the space may be dangerous and it may be safer to evacuate; follow instructions from police, fire or other local officials, who identify shelters and give directions; plan several routes; find a place that takes pets, noting that some shelters such as the American Red Cross's take only service animals; make a plan to stay in contact and expect to send messages by text or social media; go kits and medications for up to a week; check with neighbors who need a ride; call or text a friend or relative outside your area; leave a note; vehicles may not be airtight; do not go to your children, loved ones or pets unless police, fire or other local officials say it is safe, because they may be sheltered where they are; wait for the 'all clear' before returning.

entries.source_use: Meeting spot, children's contact cards, memorize numbers, learn school procedures, NCMEC hotline.

source_records.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Office of Readiness and Response)
source_records.supports: Reunification defined; faster reunion gives better outcomes for children; about 69 million children are in school or childcare on a weekday; a family plan has phone numbers, emergency contacts and multiple meeting places; schools and childcare have their own plans; contact cards for school bags; help older children memorize names and numbers; learn school drill procedures from the principal; NCMEC hotline 1-800-THE-LOST; Hurricane Katrina and Rita figures.

entries.source_use: One state's example of parent guidance; not universal.

source_records.supports: Reunification is a slow, careful process and not a normal pick-up; one state's guidance to parents: stay home and do not rush the school, wait for the school's notification of time and place, bring photo ID and a pen, limit calls and texts to keep networks open.

entries.source_use: Designate an out-of-area person as a central contact (older, undated guide).

source_records.supports: Congestion on phone networks in emergencies; limit non-emergency calls; try text messaging, which often goes through when calls do not; try multiple services; wait 10 seconds before redialing; backup power; designate an out-of-area person as central contact and make sure everyone knows who to contact; keep a corded phone that does not depend on electricity.

entries.source_use: National reunification support; archived content; Presidential declaration trigger.

source_records.supports: FEMA, the American Red Cross and NCMEC co-lead the National Reunification Committee; reunification support is triggered by Presidential emergency or major disaster declarations; NCMEC's National Emergency Child Locator Center is a call center activated at a state, tribal or territorial request for children separated from parents or guardians in a Presidentially declared disaster; NCMEC Unaccompanied Minors Registry for reporting or asking about a missing child 24 hours a day; Red Cross welfare checks via 1-800-RED CROSS; commitment to address communication access needs of people who are deaf or hard of hearing, without speech, with cognitive or intellectual disabilities, and with limited English proficiency.

entries.source_use: NCMEC's own listing of its 24-hour hotline number.

source_records.publisher: National Center for Missing & Exploited Children
source_records.supports: NCMEC's own site lists a 24-Hour Hotline and call center at 1-800-843-5678 (the numeric form of 1-800-THE-LOST); the page says that if you think you have seen a missing child, or suspect a child may be sexually exploited, you can contact NCMEC 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

entries.source_use: Out-of-state contact in the family communications plan; update the meeting place.

source_records.supports: Know your risks, destinations, zones and routes; go-bag; several destinations in different directions; pets; route may be on foot; fuel (full tank when evacuation likely, half tank at all times); one car per family; leave early; tell the out-of-state contact where you are going; leave a note; check on neighbors needing a ride; no shortcuts; after an evacuation check with officials before returning; generators outdoors only and never connected to the home's electrical system.

entries.source_use: Reconnect plan; familiar easy-to-find meeting place; document and practice.

source_records.supports: Family may not be together; know how you'll contact one another and reconnect; familiar, easy-to-find meeting place; five discussion questions (alerts, shelter plan, evacuation route, communication plan, kit); household-needs checklist (ages, medical, disabilities and access and functional needs, languages, pets, school-aged children); document and practice the plan.

entries.source_use: Fields of Ready.gov's fillable plan; not saved by any government agency.

source_records.supports: Fields of Ready.gov's family emergency communication plan: household, family members (mobile, other number or social media, email, medical information), schools, childcare, caregivers and workplaces with hotline and pick-up plan, emergency contacts, meeting places, medical information including assistive devices; stated that information entered is not saved, stored or shared by any government agency.

entries.source_use: Text messages use less bandwidth and are transmitted more reliably.

source_records.supports: Mobile networks can become overwhelmed in emergencies; text messages require less bandwidth and can be transmitted more reliably when many people are using their phones; social media and email as other ways to update family; emergency charging options at home and in the car; low-power or airplane mode to conserve battery; keep contacts updated and synced; create a group chat or thread for family; store important documents on a secure, password-protected drive or in the cloud; FEMA text commands (PREPARE, SHELTER plus ZIP code, LIST, STOP to 43362).

entries.source_use: Helper and backup assignments; practice twice a year; escape-planning rules reflected in the worksheet's checks.

source_records.supports: One or two minutes to escape; alarms in every sleeping room, outside each sleeping area and on every level; floor plan with two ways out of each room; outside meeting place a safe distance in front; assign helpers for infants, older adults and people with mobility limits, with a backup; security-bar release devices; practice twice a year; check whether children wake to the alarm; escape ladders; sealing yourself in; high-rise residents may be safer defending in place; once out, stay out.

entries.source_use: High-rise default: stairs; sealing in only when you cannot get out.

source_records.supports: Know your building's fire safety features and meet the landlord or manager about alarms, sprinklers, voice communication, evacuation plans and how to respond to an alarm; know all exit stairs from your floor; exit and stair doors marked, unlocked, unblocked; pull the alarm on the way out; feel the door before opening and close doors behind you, use another way out if hot; listen to and follow building announcements; use the stairs, typically not the elevator unless directed by the fire department, though some buildings have marked emergency-use elevators; if you cannot get out because of fire, smoke or disability: stuff wet towels or sheets around the door and vents, call the fire department and say where you are, open a window slightly and wave a bright cloth and be prepared to close the window if it makes smoke worse; fire department evacuation of a high-rise can take a long time, so communicate with the fire department.

entries.source_use: Monthly alarm test; replace the unit 10 years after manufacture.

source_records.supports: Placement (every sleeping room, outside sleeping areas, every level, 10 ft from the stove); interconnected alarms; monthly testing; replace the whole unit 10 years after manufacture; meaning of three beeps, single chirp and continued chirping; alarms for people who are deaf or hard of hearing (strobes, bed shakers).

entries.source_use: Practice in the dark; wake-up checks; simulation guidance context.

source_records.supports: A fire can become life-threatening in two minutes; smoke alarm maintenance; two ways out of each room; windows, screens and security bars; practice in the dark; teach children not to hide from firefighters; wheelchair and walker doorways; sleep with bedroom doors closed; feel doors before opening; crawl low; what to do if you cannot get out; stop, drop and roll; portable-heater and kerosene-heater tips; never use a range or oven to heat; generators never indoors.

entries.source_use: Fields of USFA's printable escape grid that the worksheet follows.

source_records.supports: Fields of USFA's printable escape plan: fire department number; draw a map or floor plan showing all windows and doors; mark two ways out of each room; choose and draw an outside meeting place in front of the home; write the fire department's emergency number on the plan; practice at least two times a year.

entries.source_use: High-rise default: leave by the stairs; cannot-get-out steps.

source_records.supports: Leave your apartment and close the door; pull the fire alarm on your way out; use the stairs, not the elevator unless directed by the fire department; go to the outside meeting place, call the fire department and say if someone is trapped; if you cannot get out because of fire, smoke or a disability: stuff wet towels or sheets around the door and vents, call 911 and tell them where you are and stay on the phone, open a window slightly and place a bright cloth outside to signal, then close the window so the air does not pull smoke into the room.

entries.source_use: Two ways out of every room; map with all doors and windows; outside meeting place in front; practice with everyone.

source_records.supports: Residents could have less than 2 minutes to escape once the smoke alarm sounds; draw a map with all doors and windows; two ways out of every room; keep doors and windows unblocked; outside meeting place in front of the home; practice with everyone; use the test button to start the drill; high-rise and condominium steps (leave and close the door, pull the alarm, use stairs not elevator unless directed, stay at the meeting place, tell the fire department if someone is trapped).

source_records.supports: Fetched the full 36-page text; read the contents list and the sections cited here (introduction, protective actions, financial preparedness, Make a Plan, supplies, documents, practice schedule). The hazard-by-hazard sections were not read. Three-step frame (know your risks, make a plan, take action); first moves when something happens without warning (assess the situation, decide to stay or change location); family communication plan with an out-of-state contact reachable two ways and a wallet or digital copy for everyone; evacuation guidelines (meeting places in several directions, half-tank rule, one car per family, leave a note); basic kit contents and the 'at least 72 hours' framing; water of 1 gallon per person per day for 3, 7 or even 14 days depending on location; cash in small bills with the highest a twenty; N95 respirators; kit maintenance (first in, first out; discard swollen, dented or corroded cans; check needs every six months); critical-document storage; practice schedule and one-year timeline.

entries.source_use: Contact list of the people who support health; check-ins; practice and annual review.

source_records.supports: List of supplies for at least a week; arrange alerts; contact list of the people who support your health, with arrangements for them to check on you directly; several places to go if you evacuate; pictures in the plan if helpful; plan for service animals and assistive technology; backup manual chair; practice the plan, review and update it every year, and share it with the people who support you.

entries.source_use: Two meeting places; text messages; microchip pets; account for children, older adults and pets.

source_records.supports: Emergency action plan with important phone numbers and at least two meeting places; microchip pets and keep registration current; have multiple ways to communicate, and text messages often go through when calls do not; plan for children, older adults and pets.

entries.source_use: Talk to a doctor or pharmacist about an emergency supply of medicines; no number of days is given.

source_records.supports: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about an emergency supply; keep a list of prescriptions with diagnosis, dosage, frequency, supply needs and allergies; nonprescription drugs; cooler and chemical ice packs for medicines that need chilling; some states have emergency prescription refill laws, so learn yours.

entries.source_use: Choose a pet-friendly place in advance because most public shelters allow only service animals.

source_records.supports: Know your risks, when and where to go, what to bring; build a go-bag so you do not scramble; everyone knows where the bag is and who is responsible; several destinations in different directions; a pet-friendly place because most public shelters allow only service animals; prepare a go-bag to carry on foot or public transport plus supplies for longer trips by car; keep a half tank at all times; one car per family; what to do before leaving; evacuation route may be on foot.

entries.source_use: The five planning questions and the list of household factors.

source_records.supports: Four steps: meet with your household (five questions: alerts, shelter, evacuation route, communication plan, kit); assess household needs (ages, responsibilities for assisting others, locations visited, dietary and medical needs, disabilities and access and functional needs, languages, cultural and religious considerations, pets or service animals, school-aged children); document the plan with the free fillable form; practice it. Family meeting place that is familiar and easy to find.

entries.source_use: Talk to your medical provider about a plan for powered medical devices and refrigerated medicine.

source_records.supports: What an extended outage can disrupt; take an inventory of items that rely on electricity; talk to your medical provider about a power-outage plan for powered medical devices and refrigerated medicines; refrigerator keeps food cold about four hours, a full freezer about 48 hours; discard food at 40 F or above for two hours or more; discard refrigerated medicine if power is out more than a day unless the label says otherwise; generators, camp stoves and charcoal grills outdoors and at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages; CO detectors with battery backup on every level; never heat a home with a gas stovetop or oven.

entries.source_use: The baseline of 1 gallon per person per day; 3 days minimum and 2 weeks as a goal; replace self-stored water every six months.

source_records.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
source_records.supports: 1 gallon per person per day for 3 days; try for 2 weeks; more for pregnancy, illness, pets, heat; container cleaning (1 tsp unscented bleach per quart, 30 seconds); replace stored water every 6 months; unscented bleach 5-9% sodium hypochlorite.

entries.source_use: That pets need several days' supply of water, with no quantity given, which is why pet and medical allowances are left for you to enter.

source_records.supports: Pets belong in the household plan; two pet kits (shelter and evacuation); store a water bowl and several days' supply of water for pets; no per-pet water quantity is given.

entries.source_use: The baseline; the statement that needs can double in very hot temperatures; the six-month replacement of non-commercial water.

source_records.supports: At least one gallon per person per day for drinking and sanitation; normal active person needs about three quarters of a gallon of fluid; more for children, nursing mothers, sick people, medical emergencies, warm climates (need can double); never ration drinking water unless ordered; avoid carbonated and caffeinated substitutes; bottled water in sealed original containers, cool and dark; replace non-commercial stored water every six months; settle or strain before treating; boiling; bleach 5.25-6% only (1/8 tsp per gallon); distillation removes microbes, heavy metals, salts and most chemicals.
